issues.legal_issue: A person claiming co-ownership of rented premises is not entitled to join an eviction suit when the dispute can be decided without that person’s presence.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought an eviction suit against tenants on grounds including non-payment of rent, subletting, and personal need.
A person claiming to be a family member and co-owner of the premises applied to join the suit as a co-plaintiff.

The eviction suit concerned whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether the pleaded grounds for eviction were established; it could be decided without resolving the applicant’s claimed ownership or share.
issues.conclusion: The applicant was neither a necessary nor a proper party to the eviction suit, and the application to join was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction suit under a rent law, the landlord and tenant are the necessary parties, and the questions are whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists and whether a ground for eviction is established; title is not germane to those questions. A plaintiff, as dominus litis, cannot be compelled to add a party unless that person is necessary or proper. A necessary party is one without whom no effective order can be made; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for a complete and final decision. Any co-owner or co-landlord may bring an eviction suit without joining all the others. The Court relied on Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Dr. Ranbir Singh v. Asharfi Lal, Ruma Chakraborty v. Sudha Rani Banerjee, Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member Board of Revenue, and Kasthuri Radhakrishnan v. M. Chinniyan.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and applicant_claimed_coownership and eviction_turns_on_tenancy_and_eviction_grounds and title_claim_cannot_be_resolved_in_proceeding and proceeding_decidable_without_applicant

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an action seeking eviction of tenants from rented premises.
predicates.applicant_claimed_coownership: A person who was not already a party claimed to co-own the premises and sought to join the action.
predicates.eviction_turns_on_tenancy_and_eviction_g: The action’s decision depended on whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether the asserted grounds for eviction were established.
predicates.title_claim_cannot_be_resolved_in_procee: The asserted ownership rights or shares between the applicant and the plaintiff were outside the questions to be decided in the eviction action.
predicates.proceeding_decidable_without_applicant: The action could be decided effectively without the applicant’s presence.

issues.definition: When an applicant claiming co-ownership seeks to join an eviction proceeding that turns on the tenancy and eviction grounds, cannot resolve the applicant’s title claim, and can be decided without the applicant, the applicant is not joined as a party.

issues.legal_issue: A determination of title made in an eviction suit does not bind an absent person claiming an interest in the premises, who may pursue an independent civil action to establish that interest.
material_facts: A person claiming co-ownership of the premises was not a party to the eviction suit.
The eviction suit was between the landlords and tenants and was not a proceeding to determine the competing ownership rights or shares of the claimant and the landlords.

The Court stated that any finding touching title in the eviction suit would not bind the absent claimant and that the claimant could bring an independent suit seeking declaration and, where appropriate, partition and separate possession.
issues.conclusion: Any finding on title in the eviction suit would not bind the absent claimant, who remained free to pursue an independent civil suit concerning the claimed property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Title to the premises is not germane to deciding an eviction suit, which concerns the landlord-tenant relationship and the grounds for eviction. Accordingly, a title finding made in that suit does not determine the rights of an absent claimant, who may seek declaratory and partition relief in an independent civil action. The Court relied on the principle stated in Dr. Ranbir Singh v. Asharfi Lal and the rules governing eviction suits under a rent law.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and claimant_absent_from_proceeding and claimant_asserts_property_interest and title_rights_outside_issues_for_decision

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an action seeking eviction of tenants from rented premises.
predicates.claimant_absent_from_proceeding: A person asserting an interest in the premises was not a party to the eviction action.
predicates.claimant_asserts_property_interest: The absent person claimed ownership or another property interest in the premises.
predicates.title_rights_outside_issues_for_decision: The competing property rights of the claimant and the landlord were not questions to be determined in the eviction action.

issues.definition: When a person asserting a property interest is absent from an eviction proceeding and that interest is outside the issues for decision, the person’s title rights are not bound and an independent action remains available.
